content: Ski sickness is a specific type of motion sickness experienced by some skiers, particularly under adverse weather conditions. This condition is often triggered by poor visibility, such as during heavy fog. The symptoms closely resemble those of other forms of motion sickness and include dizziness, headaches, and nausea. In more severe cases, vomiting may also occur. In whiteout conditions, the brain struggles to accurately interpret orientation and movement, leading to the onset of ski sickness. The condition is primarily caused by the repetitive turning motions involved in skiing, as well as other contributing factors, such as reduced sensory feedback from the feet, which are constrained by ski boots. Rudolf Häusler, a researcher from the University of Berne, estimates that up to 10% of skiers may be affected by ski sickness. Professor Häusler also discovered that over-the-counter medications commonly used to treat motion sickness are effective in alleviating the symptoms for the majority of individuals who experience this condition.
